text.text: The first ten minutes and the last ten minutes of a stay shape the review. A routine makes both feel personal, even on a busy day.
Room assigned and its requests noted on the housekeeping job
Welcome email with directions, parking, check-in time and the door code process
filled in; late arrivals get the after-hours plan
Greet by name; offer water or coffee.
Confirm dates, guests and any request (anniversary, quiet room, allergy).
Take payment for the balance or a card for incidentals, as your policy says.
Walk them to the room; show the thermostat, Wi-Fi and the best thing about that room.
Send the door code only after the booking is confirmed and paid.
Leave a welcome card with breakfast times.
Check the next morning that the room was found and all is well.
Ask how the stay was, and listen; write any problem on a repair or the guest's notes.
Settle the balance; email the receipt.
Some guests need a step-free room, a ground-floor door, or help with bags. Ask at booking, note it on the reservation, and put them in a room with
ticked. Never move such a guest to another room without asking.
Thank-you email within a day, with a link to leave a review.
Returning guests get the Returning guest rate plan and their favorite room when possible.
Theodora Aziz arrives after 9 pm on a midweek offer. Her code is sent, the Meadow King is on the turnover list, and its balcony lock repair must be done before she arrives, so it is marked urgent.
Guests judge a small hotel first by how clean it is. Clear standards, a fixed order of work and an inspection keep every room the same.
Departures that have an arrival the same day.
Stay-overs, at the time the guest asked for, or when they are out.
Public areas: breakfast room, lobby, stairs, porches.
Strip beds; fresh linens and towels
Bathroom scrubbed: shower, toilet, sink, mirror, floor; hair check
Dust surfaces, lamps, headboards, window sills
Restock: toiletries, coffee, tea, water, tissues; tick
Check lamps, remote, kettle, hair dryer; report anything broken as a repair
Air the room; set the thermostat for arrival
Make beds, empty bins, replace towels left on the floor, restock. Change linens every third night or on request. Respect "do not disturb" and offer a later time.
The innkeeper or lead housekeeper inspects every arrival room. Only an inspected room is
. Note anything missed and talk to the cleaner the same day, kindly and specifically.
. If turnovers creep past an hour, look for missing supplies or a cart that needs restocking.
Bag and label anything left behind with the room and date, then email the guest the same day. Keep unclaimed items for 60 days.
Each room gets a deep clean every 60 to 90 days: mattress flipped, curtains washed, walls wiped, grout scrubbed.
on the room shows which is next.
The Hearth Queen needs a turnover, and its last deep clean was 95 days ago. Since nobody arrives in it this week, the turnover becomes a deep clean.
In an old building something always needs fixing. Sorting repairs by how much they affect guests keeps rooms sellable and guests happy.

text.text: A room with an urgent repair that cannot be fixed goes
Anyone who sees a problem logs it: housekeeping, the front desk, or a guest.
Set the room, priority, date reported and a fix-by date.
and the date; tell the guest if they reported it.
Every room: lights, outlets, taps, toilets, locks, windows, heating and cooling
Smoke and carbon monoxide detectors tested monthly
Spring: gutters, porch and deck sealing, outdoor furniture.
Autumn: heating service, chimney sweep for rooms with fireplaces or stoves, weather-stripping.
Quiet season: painting, deep repairs, mattress replacement.

A repair past its fix-by date shows under Overdue on the Repairs list. Each morning, the innkeeper either books it, changes the date with a reason, or moves the room out of service. A repair that slips twice needs a different contractor.
Keep receipts and warranty papers with the repair. When a boiler or appliance fails twice in a year, compare the repair costs with a replacement.
Keep one plumber, electrician, heating and cooling company, handyman and locksmith on file with after-hours numbers.
Hot water pressure drops after 8 pm in the Birch Suite, which has guests. It is urgent, a plumber is booked within two days, and the guests have been offered the Loft Suite if it gets worse.
Breakfast is often the moment guests remember most at a small inn. Requests handled well turn a nice stay into a story they tell friends.
The evening before, count guests in house and any arrivals.
Prepare a menu with one hot dish, one lighter dish and a vegetarian choice; adapt for any allergy.
Serve between set hours; offer a packed breakfast for early departures.

text.text: Ask at booking and again at check-in. Keep allergy-free food apart and prepare it first. If unsure about an ingredient, do not serve it.
Count what breakfast costs per guest once a season: food, coffee, labor. If it is creeping up, simplify the menu rather than cut quality; one excellent hot dish beats three average ones.

Keep a short list of restaurants, walks and shops you know, with opening hours. Book dinner for guests when asked, and note it on their reservation, with the time, so the morning team can ask how it was.
Local chocolates or cookies on arrival
Phone chargers at the front desk
The Fairweathers, arriving in two days, asked for a vegetarian breakfast. The innkeeper plans a mushroom frittata for that morning and notes it on the reservation, so whoever cooks will see it.
A small hotel runs on three questions every morning: who is arriving, which rooms are ready, and what is broken. This workspace answers all three and keeps the numbers an innkeeper watches each week.

Last Friday and Saturday sold 8 of 8 available rooms, with the Mill Queen out of service. ADR was about 270 dollars on Friday, against about 220 on Tuesday, so the innkeeper tries a midweek offer to lift Tuesday and Wednesday.
Pricing a small hotel is a weekly habit, not a once-a-year task. The nightly report shows where rooms go empty and where you could charge more.
Each morning, enter the night before: rooms available (leave out rooms out of service), rooms sold and room revenue, without tax or breakfast extras. The formulas give occupancy, ADR and RevPAR.
